drills.q: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing actually solve, and what does it not solve?
drills.a: It solves application-layer HOL blocking (independent streams interleave over one TCP connection instead of queuing). It does NOT solve transport-layer HOL blocking: TCP delivers bytes in order across the whole connection, so one lost segment stalls every stream's data sitting behind it, even unrelated streams. On lossy networks (1-3% loss, common on cellular), this can make HTTP/2 worse than 6 independently-serialized HTTP/1.1 connections.

drills.q: Why did HTTP/1.1 pipelining fail mechanically, and how did browsers get parallelism instead?
drills.a: Responses must return in request order, so a slow response HOL-blocked faster ones behind it; middlebox/proxy bugs made it worse. No major browser enabled it by default. Instead, browsers used 6 parallel TCP connections per origin, each independently serialized (still HOL-blocked within itself) at 6x handshake/TLS/slow-start cost, sometimes multiplied further via domain sharding.

drills.q: What does HPACK actually compress and why does it matter more than people think?
drills.a: A static table of 61 common header fields plus a per-connection dynamic table (default 4096 bytes) populated as headers are actually sent -- repeated headers (cookies, Bearer tokens) get sent once in full then referenced by a small index. It matters because real API traffic resends the same several-hundred-byte auth/cookie headers on every request; over hundreds of requests per connection that's kilobytes saved, not a rounding error.

drills.q: Why did HTTP/2 server push die, and what replaced its one legitimate use case?
drills.a: It couldn't know what the client had cached, so naive implementations re-pushed already-cached assets, wasting bandwidth at scale rather than saving a round trip. Chrome disabled it by default in Chrome 106 (Oct 2022) after data showed low adoption with no consistent win. 103 Early Hints replaced the early-resource-discovery use case, letting the client decide what to fetch based on its own cache state.

drills.q: Why does HTTP/3 need a new transport (QUIC) instead of just patching TCP?
drills.a: TCP is baked into OS kernels and countless middleboxes internet-wide; evolving its core semantics requires deploying new behavior everywhere, which doesn't happen at internet scale (protocol ossification). QUIC runs over UDP and encrypts nearly the entire packet in userspace so middleboxes can't inspect or interfere with it, sidestepping the ossification problem entirely.

drills.q: How does QUIC solve transport-layer HOL blocking, and does that mean QUIC never blocks anything?
drills.a: Each QUIC stream has its own independent sequence space and loss-recovery state, unlike TCP's single ordered byte stream for the whole connection -- a lost packet belongs to one stream, only that stream stalls. It doesn't mean nothing ever blocks: it moves blocking to the correct granularity (the affected stream only); application-level cross-stream dependencies are still your own design problem.

drills.q: Compare RTT cost for a fresh connection under TCP+TLS1.2, TCP+TLS1.3, and QUIC, and explain why POST bodies can't use 0-RTT.
drills.a: TCP+TLS1.2 ~3 RTT before app data; TCP+TLS1.3 ~2 RTT; QUIC ~1 RTT for a new connection, 0-RTT for resumed connections. 0-RTT data in the first flight can be replayed by anyone who captured it since there's no fresh handshake proof yet -- safe only for idempotent/safe-to-duplicate requests, not writes like payments.

drills.q: Your team migrated to HTTP/2 and mobile p99 latency got worse. Diagnose and propose a fix -- and explain why reverting to HTTP/1.1 is wrong.
drills.a: Check packet loss on the mobile path first -- this is the classic transport-layer HOL symptom: one shared TCP connection means any loss stalls every in-flight stream, versus HTTP/1.1's 6 independent connections spreading the risk. Confirm via retransmit counts/RTT variance correlated with latency spikes across concurrent streams. The fix is HTTP/3 (per-stream loss isolation with single-connection efficiency), not reverting to HTTP/1.1, which reintroduces 6x handshake/slow-start cost as a long-term regression.

drills.q: Explain ALPN and how HTTP/3 discovery differs from HTTP/2's negotiation.
drills.a: ALPN is a TLS extension where the client advertises supported protocols (h2, http/1.1) during the TLS handshake and the server picks one -- works because both sides are already doing TCP+TLS. HTTP/3 has no equivalent bootstrap since QUIC is a separate UDP connection; instead a server advertises `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"` over an existing HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 connection, and the client caches that and tries QUIC directly on the next visit (or attempts it speculatively with a TCP fallback, a QUIC 'Happy Eyeballs' pattern).

drills.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2 and can't run on HTTP/1.1?
drills.a: gRPC needs true bidirectional streaming and multiplexing of many concurrent RPCs over one connection without one call blocking another -- exactly what HTTP/2's independent streams and framing (HEADERS/DATA/trailers) provide natively. HTTP/1.1 has no concept of concurrent streams on one connection, so you'd be back to one-request-in-flight-per-connection, defeating gRPC's design.

drills.q: Is domain sharding still a good idea under HTTP/2/3? When, if ever, is it still legitimate?
drills.a: No -- it was an HTTP/1.1-era hack to exceed the 6-connections-per-origin cap; under HTTP/2 it fragments the single-connection multiplexing benefit and HPACK's shared dynamic table, forcing extra handshakes/slow-starts you'd otherwise avoid. It remains legitimate only for reasons unrelated to connection-count (cross-origin security/CORS isolation, or genuinely serving from different geographic CDN edges) -- conflating those with the old performance hack is the mistake.

drills.q: A candidate claims 'HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking, full stop.' What's wrong with that claim, and what's the one-sentence correction?
drills.a: It's incomplete: HTTP/2 solved application-layer HOL blocking (independent streams instead of queued responses) but not transport-layer HOL blocking, since TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream for the whole connection. Correction: HTTP/2 moved HOL blocking from the application layer to the transport layer; HTTP/3 (QUIC) is what eliminates it at both layers by making streams a transport-native concept.
